rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify poorly resolved pairs while aiming for a short run. The intermediate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen the gradient while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to test whether the two weak pairs respond to slope. The current last-peak time leaves room to improve separation without exceeding 10 minutes.

The weakest pair improved substantially with a shallower gradient. Narrowing the solvent window makes the gradient shallower again, while the higher starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to make the gradient slightly shallower while bringing the late peak forward. This should lift the remaining R = 1.42 pair toward full resolution; the early peaks have ample separation to accommodate some compression.
Lower the endpoint to make the gradient shallower without further compressing the early peaks. This should improve the remaining close pair, with the last peak expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Injection 5 reached the maximum possible CRF and remains the benchmark. Increase temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation while testing the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity.

The critical pair is strongly temperature-sensitive and may separate again after reversing elution order. Test the upper temperature limit for a faster fully resolved separation, retaining injection 5 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test 55 C between the two high-temperature runs: it may separate the new early close pair while retaining the improved separation of the central cluster. This offers a plausible shorter maximum-score method than injection 5.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 C to improve the R = 1.41 pair, using the available margin before the last peak reaches 10 minutes. Monitor the central R = 1.74 pair because its reversed elution order may make it respond differently.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a shorter gradient with a higher starting organic fraction to bring the last peak forward. The early pair has some resolution margin, but both close pairs must be checked for losses from compression and altered selectivity.

Lower the starting organic fraction to restore early retention and improve the selectivity lost in injection 10. A 12-minute gradient tests whether this lower starting fraction can preserve full resolution while eluting the last peak sooner than injection 9.

Increase the endpoint to shorten elution while keeping the successful starting fraction and temperature. The early critical pair has resolution margin, and the reversed central pair may benefit from the steeper gradient.
Use the midpoint endpoint between injections 11 and 12 to recover full resolution of the R = 1.47 pair. This should retain most of the time reduction while keeping the central pair above R = 1.5.

The 55 C methods appear constrained by two competing close pairs, so test a cooler selectivity regime with a shorter gradient. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method and already achieves the maximum CRF.

Test whether a substantially steeper gradient at 60 C separates the early close pair after an elution-order reversal. The other pairs in injection 7 had useful resolution margins, making this a promising exploratory route to a much shorter separation.

Test a steeper high-temperature gradient to further separate the reversed close pair. Lowering the starting organic fraction should preserve early retention and may protect the neighboring pair from excessive compression.

Return to 55 C and test a lower starting fraction with a broader gradient. Relative to injection 12, the lower start may recover the marginal early pair while the steeper slope shortens elution; the central pair remains the main risk.

Test an intermediate temperature with a faster gradient to seek a different balance between the two selectivity-limiting pairs. Keep the low starting fraction to preserve early retention, with injection 17 retained as the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Test the unexamined 35 C selectivity regime with a moderately shallow gradient, seeking full resolution before the last peak reaches 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; this run explores an alternative to the tightly constrained 55 C methods.

Shorten injection 17’s gradient by one grid step while holding its solvent window and temperature fixed. This directly tests whether the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method can be accelerated further, though its two close pairs have little resolution margin.

Trim injection 17’s unused gradient tail while preserving its slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. All peaks should elute before the new gradient ends at the outlet, preserving maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a narrower solvent window at the proven 40 C temperature, combining a shallower slope for the central pair with a higher start to shorten retention. This explores another maximum-score method while checking that the first pair remains retained and resolved.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 22 while keeping its starting fraction and temperature fixed. This should lift the R = 1.45 pair above 1.5, with the last peak estimated to remain below 10 minutes.

Use a slope between injections 12 and 13 to balance their two limiting pairs, targeting full resolution around 7.8 minutes. This may provide more resolution margin than the fastest demonstrated method while remaining faster than injection 13.

Preserve injection 13’s successful slope and starting fraction while trimming the gradient endpoint to just above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.56. This should retain its maximum CRF and R = 1.58 minimum resolution with an 8-minute programmed gradient.
